content: The combination of lamivudine and zidovudine demonstrates synergistic antiretroviral activity against HIV-1 in MT-4 cells when used at various ratios. This synergy enhances their effectiveness in inhibiting viral replication. Lamivudine's antiviral activity against HIV-1 has been evaluated in multiple cell lines, including monocytes and fresh human peripheral blood lymphocytes, using standard susceptibility assays. The effective concentration of lamivudine required to inhibit 50% of viral replication (EC50) varies depending on the cell type, with values such as 23 mcg/mL (68 µM) in certain assays and 120 µM in peripheral blood mononuclear cells. In MT-4 cells, lamivudine has shown a 5-fold increase in activity. Zidovudine's antiviral activity against HIV-1 has also been assessed in various cell lines, including monocytes and fresh human peripheral blood lymphocytes. The EC50 for zidovudine ranges from 1 to 9 µM, depending on the assay. In studies conducted by Monogram Biosciences, the EC50 was reported as 0.0340 µM. In cell culture drug combination studies, zidovudine exhibits synergistic activity when combined with nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) such as abacavir, didanosine, lamivudine, and zalcitabine; non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) such as delavirdine and nevirapine; and protease inhibitors (PIs) such as indinavir, nelfinavir, ritonavir, and saquinavir. Zidovudine also shows additive activity when combined with interferon alfa. However, ribavirin has been found to inhibit the phosphorylation of zidovudine in cell culture, potentially reducing its efficacy. In patients receiving lamivudine monotherapy or combination therapy with lamivudine and zidovudine, HIV-1 isolates often develop resistance to lamivudine within 12 weeks. In some patients with zidovudine-resistant virus at baseline, phenotypic sensitivity to zidovudine was restored after 12 weeks of combination therapy with lamivudine and zidovudine. This combination therapy also delays the emergence of amino acid substitutions that confer resistance to zidovudine. However, prolonged therapy with lamivudine and zidovudine can lead to the emergence of HIV-1 strains resistant to both drugs. Dual resistance requires multiple amino acid substitutions, with G333E being a key mutation. The incidence of dual resistance and the duration of combination therapy required for its development remain unknown. Lamivudine-resistant HIV-1 isolates have been selected in cell culture and recovered from patients treated with lamivudine or lamivudine plus zidovudine. Genotypic analysis of these isolates reveals that resistance is associated with a specific amino acid substitution in the HIV-1 reverse transcriptase at codon 184, where methionine is replaced by either isoleucine or valine (M184V/I). Zidovudine-resistant HIV-1 isolates have also been selected in cell culture and recovered from patients treated with zidovudine. Genotypic analyses of these isolates show substitutions in the HIV-1 reverse transcriptase gene, resulting in six amino acid changes (M41L, D67N, K70R, L210W, T215Y or F, and K219Q) that confer resistance to zidovudine. Higher levels of resistance are generally associated with a greater number of amino acid substitutions. Cross-resistance among NRTIs has been observed. However, cross-resistance between lamivudine and zidovudine has not been reported. In some patients treated with lamivudine alone or in combination with zidovudine, isolates with a substitution at codon 184, conferring resistance to lamivudine, have emerged. Cross-resistance to abacavir, didanosine, tenofovir, and zalcitabine has been observed in some patients harboring lamivudine-resistant HIV-1 isolates. In patients treated with zidovudine plus didanosine or zidovudine plus zalcitabine, isolates resistant to multiple drugs, including lamivudine, have emerged. In a study of 167 HIV-1-infected patients, isolates with multi-drug resistance to didanosine, lamivudine, stavudine, zalcitabine, and zidovudine were recovered from patients treated for at least one year with zidovudine plus didanosine or zidovudine plus zalcitabine. The resistance-associated amino acid substitution pattern in these cases (A62V, V75I, F77L, F116Y, Q151M) differed from the pattern observed with zidovudine monotherapy. The Q151M substitution was most commonly associated with multi-drug resistance. The substitution at codon 151, in combination with substitutions at codons 62, 75, 77, and 116, results in a virus with reduced susceptibility to didanosine, lamivudine, stavudine, zalcitabine, and zidovudine. Thymidine analogue mutations (TAMs), selected by zidovudine, confer cross-resistance to abacavir, didanosine, stavudine, tenofovir, and zalcitabine.
